title: Preservation of Food
summary: Food is spoilt when it is no longer fit to eat: it changes colour, smells bad, shows bubbles (fermentation), mould (a spongy or powdery growth) or soft brown spots. The causes are micro-organisms, enzymes present in the food, and insects, worms and rats. Micro-organisms need air, moisture, a suitable temperature and food; they grow well in food with high moisture (tomato spoils faster than potato), in air that carries them, in food kept long at room temperature, in damaged skins, and in foods with low salt, sugar or acid (pickles, jam). Enzymes ripen fruit and then rot it. Food storage means keeping food in a suitable place till it is needed (air-tight containers, cool place).

Shelf life is the time for which food can be kept fresh. Non-perishable: whole cereals, pulses, nuts, oilseeds, sugar, jaggery. Semi-perishable: processed cereals (maida, suji), eggs, potatoes, onions, biscuits and cakes. Perishable: green leafy vegetables, peas, beans, tomatoes, apples, bananas, bread, butter, cream. Packed foods carry 'best before' or 'consume before' dates.

Preservation is a process by which food is prevented from spoiling for a short or long period, keeping colour, taste and nutritive value as far as possible. Importance: it takes care of excess produce (cheap and economical), adds variety, lets food reach places where it is not grown (deserts, snowbound regions), and makes storage and transport easier by reducing bulk (dried leafy vegetables).

Principles: (i) killing micro-organisms (boiling, pasteurisation, canning, sterilisation); (ii) preventing or delaying their action (protective covering such as skin, shell, polythene or foil; raising or lowering temperature; chemicals called preservatives); (iii) stopping enzyme action (blanching – dipping vegetables in hot water or steam for a few minutes before canning, freezing or drying).

Low temperature slows microbial and enzyme action: refrigeration 4–7 degrees C, cold storage 1–4 degrees C, freezing -18 degrees C or below. Freezing peas: shell, blanch two minutes in boiling salted water (1 teaspoon salt per half litre), drain, cool 10–15 minutes, pack in strong polythene bags, remove air, seal and freeze. Precautions: strong bags, small packets, do not refreeze thawed food, exclude air; stored up to six months.

High temperature: pasteurisation heats food (milk) to a high temperature and cools it quickly, killing most but not all micro-organisms; sterilisation exposes food or bottles to high temperature for longer, sometimes under pressure, destroying all micro-organisms.

Preservatives are substances added to make food last longer. Natural: salt (osmosis draws water out; pickles, fish), sugar (dissolves in the water of the food so less water is available; jam, jelly, squash), acids (lemon juice, vinegar, citric acid), oil and spices (oil covers pickle and keeps out air and micro-organisms; mustard, turmeric, chilli). Chemical: sodium benzoate, potassium metabisulphite (KMS), citric acid (ketchup, squash, chips, jam). Apple jam: apples 1 kg, sugar 750 g, citric acid 1 teaspoon, water 150 ml; cook, sieve, add sugar and citric acid, cook to a gel-like consistency, test by dropping jam in ice-cold water (it should solidify in one place), pour hot into sterilised wide-mouthed bottles. Orange squash: juice 1 litre, sugar 2 kg, water 1 litre, citric acid 30 g, KMS half teaspoon, essence and colour; boil sugar, water and citric acid, add juice, add KMS dissolved in a little juice, bottle in sterilised bottles and store in a cool place away from sun.

Dehydration removes water or moisture (methi, pudina, cauliflower, amla, raw mango, potato chips, papad, wadis, vermicelli). Steps: clean and sun-dry the tins and trays; wash and cut vegetables, removing stems, seeds and decayed parts; blanch; dip in cold water with salt and KMS for 5–10 minutes to stop blackening (not for green leafy vegetables as KMS bleaches them); spread on a clean cloth in strong sun covered with thin cloth; cool and store in air-tight containers.

Keep utensils and containers clean and sun-dried, with air-tight lids; keep a layer of oil above pickles; use clean dry spoons and close the lid at once; sterilise sauce and squash bottles by heating them in water for 30–40 minutes.

vsa: Which four precautions will you adopt while freezing peas at home?

Use strong polythene bags that can bear expansion; make small packets so thawed food is used at once; do not refreeze food once it has thawed; remove all air before sealing. (Also blanch the peas before freezing.)
April 2026

or: Your brother has washed and cut apples. Tell him further procedure to make jam.

Cook the pieces in water until tender (or pressure cook for 2 minutes); sieve the pulp; add sugar (750 g for 1 kg apples) and citric acid; cook to a thick consistency, testing by dropping jam in ice-cold water – if it solidifies in one place it is ready; pour hot into sterilised wide-mouthed bottles and store in a cool place.

vsa: Analyse any three conditions appropriate for the growth of micro-organisms.

Micro-organisms grow in food with high moisture, in food kept for a long time at room temperature, in damaged skin of fruits and vegetables, in air carrying them, and in food with low salt, sugar or acid.
October 2025
What does food preservation mean? Why is it important?

Preservation is a process by which food is prevented from spoiling for a short or long time while its colour, taste and nutritive value are kept as far as possible. It takes care of excess produce, adds variety, sends food to places where it is not grown and makes storage and transport easier.
October 2022
Name any four household methods of food preservation.
Refrigeration or freezing; boiling or pasteurisation; dehydration or sun drying; use of salt, sugar, oil, spices or acids as in pickles, jams and squashes (any four).
April 2023
Give any four ways to delay the action of micro-organisms on apples.
Do not remove the peel; pack in polythene or aluminium foil; keep in the refrigerator; make jam; dehydrate.
How does salt act as a preservative?
Salt draws water out of the food by osmosis. With little water the micro-organisms cannot grow, and salt also reduces enzyme activity. This is why pickles, chutneys and fish are salted.
Using the apple jam recipe (apples 1 kg, sugar 750 g, citric acid 1 teaspoon, water 150 ml), find the quantities needed for 2 kg of apples.
Everything is doubled for 2 kg of apples. Sugar = 750 g x 2 = 1500 g (1.5 kg); citric acid = 1 teaspoon x 2 = 2 teaspoons; water = 150 ml x 2 = 300 ml.
Why are green leafy vegetables not put in KMS solution before drying?
Potassium metabisulphite bleaches the colour of green leafy and other dark vegetables, so they lose their natural colour.
sa: Write the steps of preserving cauliflower or methi by the dehydration method (any six points).

(1) Clean and sun-dry all trays and tins. (2) Wash and cut the vegetable; remove stems and any decaying part. (3) Blanch in boiling water until slightly soft (reduces enzyme action); for cauliflower dip in cold salt and KMS solution for 5–10 minutes to prevent blackening (not for methi). (4) Spread on a clean cloth in strong sun. (5) Cover with a thin cloth to keep off dust and flies. (6) When dry, cool and store in air-tight containers.
Explain the three principles of food preservation with one example of each.

(i) Killing micro-organisms – boiling or pasteurising milk, canning. (ii) Preventing or delaying their action – a protective covering such as polythene or foil, freezing in a refrigerator, adding preservatives like salt or sugar. (iii) Stopping the action of enzymes – blanching vegetables in hot water or steam before freezing or drying; heating milk.
How will you prepare orange squash from one litre of orange juice?

Take 1 litre juice, 2 kg sugar, 1 litre water, 30 g citric acid, half teaspoon KMS, essence and colour. Boil water, sugar and citric acid until the sugar dissolves; add colour, essence and juice. Dissolve KMS in a little juice and mix it in. Pour into sterilised bottles, cool, seal tightly and store in a cool place away from sun.

or: Guide your sister regarding the steps to freeze one kg of peas at home.

Shell the peas; boil salted water (1 teaspoon salt for half a litre) and immerse the peas for about two minutes; drain immediately in a sieve and cool for 10–15 minutes; pack in small strong polythene bags, press out the air and seal; put the packets in the freezer. Do not refreeze thawed peas.

sa: Guide your sister to make potato chips at home.

Wash, peel and cut potatoes into thin slices; put them in boiling water for 3–4 minutes (blanching); make a solution in cold water with 5 teaspoons salt and 1 teaspoon KMS (for 5 kg potatoes) and keep the slices in it for 10 minutes; spread each slice separately on a cloth in the sun and cover with a thin cloth; when dry, cool and store in air-tight containers.
la: Explain any five points on the importance of food preservation and name two foods preserved at home.

(1) It takes care of excess produce, which would otherwise rot and cause loss to farmers. (2) Foods preserved in season are cheap and economical. (3) It adds variety to meals, e.g. peas or cauliflower in the off-season. (4) Preserved foods can be sent to places where they are not grown, such as deserts and snowbound areas. (5) Drying reduces bulk and makes storage and transport easy. Examples: mango pickle, jam, squash, dried methi, papad.
Describe the use of natural and chemical preservatives in food preservation with examples.

Natural preservatives: salt (pickle, chutney, fish; draws out water), sugar (jam, jelly, squash; reduces available water), acids such as lemon juice, vinegar and citric acid (pickles, ketchup, squash), and oil and spices (oil covers pickle and keeps out air and micro-organisms). Chemical preservatives: sodium benzoate, potassium metabisulphite and citric acid, used in jam, squash, ketchup and chips. Usually a combination of principles is used, e.g. salt, spices and oil in pickle; sugar and acid in squash.
